title: Content Delivery Network
description: Design a CDN — routing users to nearby edge servers, caching hierarchies, cache keys and invalidation, origin shielding, and handling flash crowds.
author: Editorial Team

blocks.title: What is a CDN?
blocks.text: A content delivery network is a global fleet of edge servers that cache content — images, video, scripts, API responses — close to users, so requests travel tens of kilometres instead of across oceans, and origin servers handle a fraction of the traffic.

items: Customers should be able to put a CDN in front of their origin for a domain.
Users requesting content should be served from a nearby edge server.
Edges should cache content according to cache rules (TTLs, headers) and fetch misses from the origin.
Customers should be able to purge (invalidate) content globally.

blocks.question: What are the non-functional requirements for this system?

items: Low latency: most users within ~20-50ms of an edge.
High cache hit ratio (95%+ for static content) to protect origins.
Highly available: an edge or whole location failing shouldn't cause errors.
**PoP (point of presence)**: a location with many edge servers.
**Cache object**: a response stored under a cache key (host + path + selected headers/query) with TTL.
**Configuration**: per-customer cache rules, origins and certificates.

blocks.text: 1) Route users to a nearby edge

items: **Anycast**: every PoP announces the same IP addresses via BGP; the internet routes each user to the topologically nearest PoP.
**DNS-based routing**: the CDN's DNS returns the IP of a PoP chosen by the resolver's location, latency measurements and PoP load.

blocks.text: Each edge server checks its cache (memory for hot objects, SSD for the rest). On a miss it fetches from a regional **shield** PoP, which in turn fetches from the origin. Responses are cached according to `Cache-Control` headers or customer rules.
Purge requests go to the control plane, which fans out invalidation messages to every PoP via a global pub/sub system; edges drop or mark matching objects stale.
1) How do we maximise hit ratio and protect the origin?

blocks.title: Every edge fetches misses from origin

approach.text: Each of thousands of edge servers goes straight to the origin on a miss.

challenges.text: A newly popular object causes thousands of simultaneous origin requests.

approach.text: Within a PoP, hash the cache key to choose which server stores an object, so the PoP holds one copy instead of one per server — effectively a much larger cache.

challenges.text: Doesn't stop every PoP from separately fetching from origin.

blocks.title: Tiered caching with origin shield + request collapsing

approach.text: Route misses through a small number of regional **shield** PoPs, so the origin sees roughly one request per object per region. At every tier, **collapse concurrent misses** for the same key into a single upstream fetch while others wait. Serve stale content while revalidating (`stale-while-revalidate`) and if the origin is down (`stale-if-error`).

challenges.text: An extra hop on misses; worth it for hit ratio and origin protection.

blocks.text: 2) How do we design cache keys and invalidation?

Cache keys must include only what changes the response: host, path, and selected query parameters or headers (e.g. `Accept-Encoding`). Including unnecessary values (tracking query strings, cookies) fragments the cache. For invalidation, prefer **versioned URLs** (`app.3f9a.js`) that never need purging; use purge for mistakes and urgent removals, propagated through a global message bus with acknowledgements from each PoP.

Health-check edges and PoPs continuously. With anycast, a failed PoP withdraws its route and traffic shifts automatically; with DNS routing, the control plane stops returning that PoP. Within a PoP, load balancers remove unhealthy servers.

quiz.question: What does an origin shield do?
options: Funnels misses through a regional tier so the origin sees far fewer requests
quiz.explanation: Shields consolidate cache misses before they reach the origin.

quiz.question: What is request collapsing?
options: Combining concurrent misses for the same object into one upstream fetch
quiz.explanation: It prevents stampedes on newly popular content.

quiz.question: Why are versioned asset URLs preferred over purges?
options: A new version gets a new URL, so no invalidation is needed
quiz.explanation: Immutable URLs can be cached forever safely.

quiz.question: How does anycast route users?
options: All PoPs announce the same IPs and BGP routes users to the nearest one
quiz.explanation: Network routing itself picks the closest PoP.
